edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 50's title, “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0 = oshb:Ps.50.1), sits inside MT verse 1 as an identity psalm; the verse continues directly into the theophany's opening triple divine name, אֵ֤ל אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים יְֽהוָ֗ה (El, Elohim, YHWH) (oshb:Ps.50.1). The narrated theophany — “Our God comes, and does not keep silent. A fire devours before him. It is very stormy around him.” (web:Ps.50.3) — runs in third-person narration through the embedded summons “"Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice."” (web:Ps.50.5) and closes with the narrator's own comment, “The heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge. Selah.” (web:Ps.50.6), before direct divine speech to the people begins at the next seam.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 50:9 to include the opening lines of God's speech was considered, but the addressee changes from third-person narration about God to first-person divine self-address beginning at 50:7, which belongs to the next span.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.1 stacks three divine names (אֵ֤ל, אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים, יְֽהוָ֗ה) before any verb of speech
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, the row's closing verse
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 50 functions as the single parent grouping. Its title “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0) carries the mizmor and le-Asaph labels; Ps 50 is Book II's sole le-Asaph psalm (1 of 12), with the other 11 le-Asaph psalms sitting in Book III (73-83); this is a divine-lawsuit psalm whose three speech frames (narration, address to the covenant people, address to the wicked) organize the rows below.

edited_rows.rationale: Direct divine speech to the covenant people opens with the self-identification formula “"Hear, my people, and I will speak. Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God.” (web:Ps.50.7), where OSHB stacks אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֱלֹהֶ֣יךָ אָנֹֽכִי (God, your God, I) as the speech-frame marker (oshb:Ps.50.7). This is the first of the psalm's 2 divine discourse blocks introduced by an explicit narrator speech formula (oshb:Ps.50.7, oshb:Ps.50.16), distinct from the embedded first-person summons at oshb:Ps.50.5, and runs through the sacrifice polemic — “I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens.” (web:Ps.50.9) — to the positive instruction that closes it, “Offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving. Pay your vows to the Most High.” (web:Ps.50.14). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.50.6) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the frame shift, not a driver in its own right.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting this speech at the anaphoric ‘mine’ sequence of 50:10-12 (the animals of the forest, the wild animals, the world) was considered, but that repetition is rhetorical elaboration within one unbroken first-person speech, not a new speech-frame or addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.7 opens with the imperative שִׁמְעָ֤ה (Hear) matching the psalm's own opening summons register
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, immediately preceding this span's start
edited_rows.device_notes: The psalm's earlier divine speech, addressed to ‘my people’; its close at 50:14-15 anticipates the psalm's final line (50:23).

edited_rows.rationale: A new speech frame opens with an explicit narrator formula, “But to the wicked God says, "What right do you have to declare my statutes, that you have taken my covenant on your lips,” (web:Ps.50.16), where OSHB marks the addressee change directly: וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים — ‘but to the wicked, God said’ (oshb:Ps.50.16). This rebuke runs through the closing appeal, “"Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you into pieces, and there be no one to deliver.” (web:Ps.50.22), and ends on “Whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies me, and prepares his way so that I will show God's salvation to him."” (web:Ps.50.23), which repeats the phrase “the sacrifice of thanksgiving” from web:Ps.50.14, framing the whole psalm.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating 50:22-23 as a separate closing unit was considered, since ‘Now consider this’ shifts from accusation to appeal, but the same addressee and speech-frame continue across that shift, unlike the explicit dixit formula opening at 50:16.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.16 opens with the explicit speech-frame formula וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים, reintroducing direct divine speech to a new addressee
edited_rows.device_notes: Second divine speech, addressed to ‘the wicked’; its close echoes the sacrifice-of-thanksgiving instruction of 50:14, an inclusio internal to the psalm.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 51's title carries the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note, “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.1, web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.2), and the psalm opens with the imperative petition “Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.” (web:Ps.51.1), doubled by “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.” (web:Ps.51.2), where OSHB pairs the qere הֶ֭רֶב (a ketiv/qere pair at oshb:Ps.51.4; the rbh root, ‘greatly/thoroughly’) with the wash-root proper, כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (‘wash me’, oshb:Ps.51.4), the same root recurring as תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי at oshb:Ps.51.9. The petition grounds itself in confession — “Against you, and you only, I have sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight, so you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.” (web:Ps.51.4), whose Hebrew opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮ ‘against you, you alone’ (oshb:Ps.51.6) — through the admission “Behold, I was born in iniquity. My mother conceived me in sin.” (web:Ps.51.5) and closes on the wisdom claim “Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (web:Ps.51.6), before the volitive-petition register resumes at the next seam.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Breaking after 51:2 (petition) from 51:3-6 (confession) was considered, since the register shifts from imperative to indicative there, but both halves address God without any vocative or speech-frame change, so they are kept as one petition-grounded-in-confession movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.6 opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮, fronting the second-person object before the verb of sinning

oshb:Ps.51.4's כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (‘wash me’) anticipates the same wash-root's reuse as תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי (oshb:Ps.51.9) at the next span's opening petition (51:7); oshb:Ps.51.4 also carries a ketiv/qere pair (ketiv הרבה, qere הֶ֭רֶב) undisclosed elsewhere in this row
edited_rows.device_notes: One composition, Psalm 51, parents this row set. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0) carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and le-David labels plus the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note; this +2 psalm's rows dual-cite both MT title verses at this, the opening row; the psalm's other three rows (146-148) do not repeat the title dual-cite.

edited_rows.rationale: A cluster of renewal petitions opens “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.” (web:Ps.51.7), where OSHB's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי (‘wash me’, a prefix-conjugation volitive, oshb:Ps.51.9) reuses the wash-root already voiced as the true imperative כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי at oshb:Ps.51.4 (see the seam at 51:6|51:7; that verse's הֶ֭רֶב is a separate ketiv/qere token, the rbh intensifier, not the wash-root), and continues through the imperative pair “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (web:Ps.51.10), where OSHB pairs לֵ֣ב טָ֭הוֹר בְּרָא לִ֣י — ‘a clean heart create for me’ (oshb:Ps.51.12) — to the closing petition “Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.” (web:Ps.51.12), where OSHB opens הָשִׁ֣יבָה (‘restore’, an imperative, oshb:Ps.51.14). The span is a dense cluster of renewal petitions, the strongest of the psalm's 3 internal seams by imperative density.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the span through 51:13 (‘Then I will teach transgressors’) was considered, since it continues the first-person address to God, but 51:13 shifts from imperative petition to a cohortative vow of future action, which belongs with the psalm's next movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.9's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי repeats the wash-root of oshb:Ps.51.4's כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (not the ketiv/qere token הֶ֭רֶב at the same verse, which is the separate rbh intensifier)

oshb:Ps.51.12 opens with its fronted object לֵ֣ב טָ֭הוֹר (“a clean heart”, web:Ps.51.10), with the verb בְּרָא (‘create’) as the third token — the verse quoted as “Create in me a clean heart” at web:Ps.51.10
edited_rows.device_notes: Renewal-petition cluster; re-derived from source bytes: 5 true imperative-form tokens across 3 of this span's 6 verses — hide, blot out (web:Ps.51.9); create, renew (web:Ps.51.10); restore (web:Ps.51.12) — excluding the taw-preformative prefix forms that open web:Ps.51.7 (purify, wash), which read as volitive petitions rather than true imperatives. oshb:Ps.51.3-Ps.51.4 independently carry 5 imperative tokens across those 2 verses, so this span is not, by that count, the psalm's highest imperative concentration.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalmist's voice turns from petition to vow, “Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Sinners will be converted to you.” (web:Ps.51.13), where OSHB's אֲלַמְּדָ֣ה (“I will teach”, a 1cs cohortative with paragogic he, oshb:Ps.51.15) opens the verse, and moves through the plea “Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God, the God of my salvation. My tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.” (web:Ps.51.14) and “Lord, open my lips. My mouth will declare your praise.” (web:Ps.51.15) into a theological claim about sacrifice, “For you don't delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering.” (web:Ps.51.16), closing “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (web:Ps.51.17). This unit's cohortative-vow opening and its sacrifice-theology close both mark it off from the imperative cluster before it and the Zion petition after it.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding 51:16-17's sacrifice theology into the closing Zion petition (51:18-19) was considered, since both touch on sacrifice, but 51:16-17 argues against animal sacrifice in the first person while 51:18-19 shifts to imperative petition for the city.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.51.13 opens with a first-person cohortative (“I will teach”), a register shift from the imperative cluster of 51:7-12
edited_rows.device_notes: Vow-and-sacrifice-theology unit; its claim that God is not pleased with sacrifice sets up the debated petition that follows.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm closes with an imperative petition for the city, “Do well in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem.” (web:Ps.51.18), where OSHB names צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה — ‘Zion—you will build’ (oshb:Ps.51.20) — and resolves in “Then you will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and in whole burnt offerings. Then they will offer bulls on your altar.” (web:Ps.51.19). The topographic naming of Zion and Jerusalem's walls, absent from the rest of the psalm, marks this as a distinct closing unit.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading 51:18-19 as continuous with 51:13-17 rather than a separate unit is the mandated rival: commentators disagree on whether the Zion petition is integral to the psalm or a later liturgical addition responding to Jerusalem's walls being broken, since the verse names actual city walls rather than speaking figuratively of the individual penitent. The candidate holds it as its own unit given its topographic register shift (see observed_substrate_signals), but the seam is registered as uncertain.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.20 (web:Ps.51.18) is the sole occurrence in the psalm of צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה (‘Zion—you will build’; sweep: 1 verse); the standalone lexeme צִיּ֑וֹן (Zion) likewise occurs only here in the psalm (sweep: 1 verse)
edited_rows.device_notes: Closing Zion petition; a debated seam (see rejected_alternative) held here as its own low-confidence unit.

edited_rows.rationale: The address shifts from second-person accusation to third-person report, “The righteous also will see it, and fear, and laugh at him, saying,” (web:Ps.52.6), where OSHB opens with וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים (‘and-they-will-see the-righteous’, oshb:Ps.52.8), and quotes their verdict, “"Behold, this is the man who didn't make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness."” (web:Ps.52.7). The psalmist's own first-person voice then closes the psalm, “But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in God's house. I trust in God's loving kindness forever and ever.” (web:Ps.52.8) and “I will give you thanks forever, because you have done it. I will hope in your name, for it is good, in the presence of your saints.” (web:Ps.52.9). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.52.5) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the addressee shift, not a driver in its own right.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting 52:6-7 (the righteous' reported speech) from 52:8-9 (the psalmist's own testimony) was considered: WEB does close the quoted speech at the end of web:Ps.52.7, and oshb:Ps.52.10 (=web:Ps.52.8) does open with the contrastive independent pronoun וַאֲנִ֤י, a genuine speech-frame terminus and pivot — a real seam, not an absence. The split was nonetheless rejected because both halves share the same third-person-then-first-person vantage against the wicked man of 52:1-5, which the row treats as the stronger, unifying warrant at this length.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.52.5, immediately preceding this span's start
oshb:Ps.52.8 opens וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים, marking the addressee shift from second to third person
edited_rows.device_notes: Closing unit: the righteous' verdict on the wicked man, then the psalmist's contrasting self-testimony ‘like a green olive tree.’

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 53 is a short, indivisible movement of six WEB verses and is chunked as one row per book policy. Its title, “For the Chief Musician. To the tune of "Mahalath." A contemplation by David.” (web:Ps.53.0 = oshb:Ps.53.1), opens directly into “The fool has said in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity. There is no one who does good.” (web:Ps.53.1), where OSHB reads אָ֘מַ֤ר נָבָ֣ל בְּ֭לִבּוֹ אֵ֣ין — ‘said [the] fool in-his-heart, there-is-no God’ (oshb:Ps.53.2) — and the poem runs one unbroken argument through the divine survey, “God looks down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there are any who understood, who seek after God.” (web:Ps.53.2), the universal verdict, “Every one of them has gone back. They have become filthy together. There is no one who does good, no, not one.” (web:Ps.53.3), and the closing hope for Israel's restoration, “Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! When God brings back his people from captivity, then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.” (web:Ps.53.6), where OSHB's mi-yitten optative idiom מִ֥י יִתֵּ֣ן (‘oh that—will give’) opens the verse, naming מִצִּיּוֹן֮ (Zion) and יִשְׂרָ֫אֵ֥ל (Israel) around the construct-plural יְשֻׁע֪וֹת (‘salvation(s) of’) (oshb:Ps.53.7).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting 53:1-3 (the universal indictment) from 53:4-6 (address to the ‘workers of iniquity’ and closing hope) was considered given the six-verse length is at the edge of the book's whole-psalm threshold, but no vocative or speech-frame shift marks an internal seam, and the psalm reads as one movement.
observed_substrate_signals: skeleton sweep of this psalm's WEB span (53:1-6, MT 53:2-7) finds Elohim seven times across five of its six verses and YHWH zero times (sweep: 7 occurrences, 5 verses; oshb:Ps.53.3, oshb:Ps.53.6) — independently re-derived from the bytes, matching the book's Elohistic-Psalter inventory
edited_rows.device_notes: Grouped, the rows answer to Psalm 53 alone. Psalm 53 stands in a typed doublet relation with Psalm 14 (an Elohistic recension of the same composition, per the book's doublet inventory); this row addresses Psalm 53's own text and makes no byte claim about Psalm 14. The Elohim-for-YHWH substitution is this psalm's own Elohistic-Psalter texture, legitimate discussion but not a boundary driver, since the psalm is chunked whole.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 54 coheres as one liturgical composition, and this row reports to one parent. The historical-note title fixes the setting: the Ziphites' report to Saul, “Isn't David hiding himself among us?” (web:Ps.54.0 = oshb:Ps.54.1) — and the seven verses that follow run one continuous movement: an imperative plea (web:Ps.54.1), a grounding complaint closed by Selah (web:Ps.54.3), and a vow-and-report close (web:Ps.54.6-Ps.54.7), with no internal address shift strong enough at this length to warrant a split.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting at the Selah (web:Ps.54.3) into a plea half and a vow half was rejected: the psalm runs seven verses, under the short-psalm threshold, and Selah is capped at tier-3 corroboration by policy, not treated as a driver alone.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative doublet “Save me, God, by your name. Vindicate me in your might” opens the psalm (web:Ps.54.1)
a Selah closes the complaint before the vow (web:Ps.54.3)
the closing verse pairs deliverance with a report clause, “My eye has seen triumph over my enemies” (web:Ps.54.7)
edited_rows.device_notes: The title carries maskil, lamnatseach, and le-David labels (tier-1 opener evidence) alongside the Ziphite historical note; Book II runs Elohim-heavy here (unsuffixed Elohim in 4 verses, one token each, oshb:Ps.54.3-54.6 / unsuffixed YHWH in 1 verse, oshb:Ps.54.8), matching the Elohistic Psalter texture at this position in the book.

edited_rows.rationale: One parent gathers Psalm 55's rows: the composition itself. This strophe opens on direct address to God — “Listen to my prayer, God. Don't hide yourself from my supplication” (web:Ps.55.1) — and holds together as the psalmist's inner-turmoil report through the wish to flee, “Oh that I had wings like a dove! Then I would fly away, and be at rest” (web:Ps.55.6), continuing past an interior Selah into the shelter-wish of web:Ps.55.8 before the seam: the next verse turns to an imperative against the enemy's city rather than the self.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Closing the strophe at web:Ps.55.7, where the Selah sits, was rejected: WEB punctuates web:Ps.55.6-Ps.55.7 and web:Ps.55.8 as two separate quotations, but MT carries no closing marker between them, and the flight-wish “I would hurry to a shelter” (web:Ps.55.8) reads as one continuous wish with the Selah falling interior to it rather than at its edge.
observed_substrate_signals: vocative-plus-imperative pair “Listen...Don't hide” opens the psalm (web:Ps.55.1)
a Selah sits mid-quote, before the wish resumes (web:Ps.55.7)
the quoted wish runs continuously from web:Ps.55.6 through web:Ps.55.8
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 55 carries a maskil, lamnatseach, le-David title with no historical note; its rows track a plea, betrayal, confidence, and verdict movement.

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe opens on a fresh imperative address, “Confuse them, Lord, and confound their language, for I have seen violence and strife in the city” (web:Ps.55.9), pivots at web:Ps.55.12's “For it was not an enemy who insulted me” into naming the betrayer as “a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend” (web:Ps.55.13), and closes on an imprecation grounded in a ketiv/qere pair (oshb:Ps.55.16: ketiv ישימות, qere יַשִּׁ֤י מָ֨וֶת), “Let death come suddenly on them” (web:Ps.55.15).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A seam between web:Ps.55.11 and web:Ps.55.12, separating the city-violence description from the betrayer's naming, was rejected: web:Ps.55.12's “For” argues directly from the city description to the betrayer's identity within one continuous accusation.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative “Confuse them, Lord” opens the strophe (web:Ps.55.9)
the causal pivot “For it was not an enemy” marks the turn to the betrayer (web:Ps.55.12)
the strophe closes on an imprecation, “go down alive into Sheol” (web:Ps.55.15)

edited_rows.rationale: An explicit contrastive turn opens the strophe, “As for me, I will call on God. Yahweh will save me” (web:Ps.55.16), moving through confidence in being heard (web:Ps.55.17-Ps.55.18) to a verdict on the unrepentant at web:Ps.55.19, where the psalm's second Selah sits mid-verse (token 6 of 13 in oshb:Ps.55.20) as corroboration; the verdict clause following it, together with the referent's narrowing from the unrepentant “them” to a specific “he” at the seam with web:Ps.55.20, are what actually close this strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe through web:Ps.55.20 was rejected: web:Ps.55.20 returns the subject to a specific “he” (the betrayer) rather than the “them” of web:Ps.55.19's verdict, marking a fresh referent shift.
observed_substrate_signals: contrastive self-reference “As for me” opens the strophe (web:Ps.55.16)

a Selah (oshb:Ps.55.20) sits mid-verse in the strophe's closing verse (token 6 of 13), corroborating rather than driving the boundary; the verdict clause and the referent-narrowing at the seam with web:Ps.55.20 are the actual drivers

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe's front seam carries the psalm's second Selah, sitting mid-verse in web:Ps.55.19 (token 6 of 13 in oshb:Ps.55.20) as corroboration for the prior verdict's close, before this unit resumes on a specific referent, “He raises his hands against his friends. He has violated his covenant” (web:Ps.55.20), and closes the psalm on a contrastive turn to trust, “But you, God, will bring them down into the pit of destruction...but I will trust in you” (web:Ps.55.23).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.55.20-Ps.55.23 as a continuation of the prior strophe, rather than its own unit, was rejected: the shift from “them” (the verdict's plural target) to “he” (a specific betrayer) reopens the friend-betrayal thread named at web:Ps.55.13.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe's front-seam verse carries the psalm's second Selah (web:Ps.55.19)
the referent narrows from plural “them” to singular “he” at the seam (web:Ps.55.19-Ps.55.20)
the closing verse turns on a contrastive “But you, God...but I will trust in you” (web:Ps.55.23)

edited_rows.rationale: Both rows of Psalm 56 report to one parent grouping for the psalm. This strophe opens the historical-note title's setting — “when the Philistines seized him in Gath” (web:Ps.56.0 = oshb:Ps.56.1) — into a plea, “Be merciful to me, God, for man wants to swallow me up” (web:Ps.56.1), and holds the complaint through a trust declaration, “In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (web:Ps.56.4), before the seam returns to the enemies' conspiracy (web:Ps.56.5-Ps.56.7).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Isolating web:Ps.56.4 as its own row was rejected: the trust declaration's return is split across web:Ps.56.10-Ps.56.11 later in the psalm rather than repeated whole here, so this occurrence functions as an interior turn within the strophe, not an edge.
observed_substrate_signals: the trust declaration “In God, I praise his word” (web:Ps.56.4) recurs, reworded, at web:Ps.56.10-Ps.56.11
the strophe closes back on the enemies' conspiracy, “They conspire and lurk, watching my steps” (web:Ps.56.6 = oshb:Ps.56.7; ketiv יצפינו, qere יִצְפּ֗וֹנוּ)
edited_rows.device_notes: The title carries miktam, lamnatseach, le-David labels plus the al-yonat-elem tune name (“Silent Dove in Distant Lands”, web:Ps.56.0) and a historical note — distinct from the al-tashcheth tune shared by Psalms 57, 58, 59, and 75.

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe opens on a shift to divine record-keeping, “You count my wanderings. You put my tears into your container. edited_rows.rationale: The parent for both of Psalm 58's rows is the composition itself. This strophe opens on a rhetorical question addressed to a debated vocative — WEB renders it “silent ones”, “Do you indeed speak righteousness, silent ones?” (web:Ps.58.1), underneath which the Hebrew term אֵ֣לֶם (the second token of oshb:Ps.58.2, after the interrogative particle הַֽאֻמְנָ֗ם) is read here as a lexical crux rather than resolved to one sense — moves through the wicked's nature from birth (web:Ps.58.3-Ps.58.4), and closes where the cobra image of web:Ps.58.4 completes its own figure, “which doesn't listen to the voice of charmers, no matter how skillful the charmer may be” (web:Ps.58.5), where OSHB's אֲשֶׁ֣ר (‘which’, oshb:Ps.58.6) opens a subordinate relative clause rather than independent material.

Selah closes web:Ps.60.4 (oshb:Ps.60.6), but the unit runs one verse further: (oshb:Ps.60.7) לְ֭מַעַן יֵחָלְצ֣וּן is a למען purpose clause completing the banner-display of web:Ps.60.4 rather than opening independent material, so the petition’s imperative arrives in web:Ps.60.5, “save with your right hand, and answer us”. A ketiv/qere note sits at the close of this span (oshb:Ps.60.7): the unpointed ketiv (oshb:Ps.60.7) ועננו beside the pointed qere (oshb:Ps.60.7) וַעֲנֵֽנִי — the kq inventory’s one entry in Ps 60.

edited_rows.rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.62.0 = oshb:Ps.62.1), naming the Jeduthun setting (one of 3 Ps psalms so labeled, with Psalms 39 and 77). The unit is a ring: it opens on (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה “My soul rests in God alone” (web:Ps.62.1), turns at web:Ps.62.3 to a complaint against attackers, “How long will you assault a man?”, and returns to the same confidence idiom at (oshb:Ps.62.6) אַ֣ךְ לֵ֭אלֹהִים דּ֣וֹמִּי נַפְשִׁ֑י “My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.” (web:Ps.62.5), completing the envelope. Collated against oshb:Ps.62.6, oshb:Ps.62.2 shares no tier — real lexical substitution: (oshb:Ps.62.2) אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים against (oshb:Ps.62.6) לֵ֭אלֹהִים, and (oshb:Ps.62.2) יְשׁוּעָתִֽי against (oshb:Ps.62.6) תִּקְוָתִֽי — so the return is thematic anaphora (sweep: 6 verses open with אך in Ps 62, 34 book-wide), not a repeated line.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the ring at its individual אך-openings into separate one- or two-verse rows was rejected, since the confidence-complaint-confidence pattern needs the full envelope to complete, not one opening on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: אך opens (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ, oshb:Ps.62.3, and (oshb:Ps.62.5) אַ֤ךְ inside this row, plus 2 more later in the psalm: 6 verse-initial occurrences of אך among Ps 62’s 12 MT body verses; a separate contiguous-consonantal-substring sweep finds 34 occurrences book-wide.

oshb:Ps.62.3 opens with אַךְ ה֣וּא צ֭וּרִי, echoed at this row’s own closing verse, oshb:Ps.62.7 (=web:Ps.62.6), which opens with the same 3 words at skeleton tier; oshb:Ps.62.3 carries a closing word oshb:Ps.62.7 lacks.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.4 (oshb:Ps.62.5), mid-ring rather than at the row’s own end — disclosed, not treated as the driver.
edited_rows.device_notes: This row family has Psalm 62 for its parent.

edited_rows.rationale: This unit opens still in first-person voice, continuing the rock vocabulary of the prior row's close: “My salvation and my honor is with God. The rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.” (web:Ps.62.7), where OSHB's צוּר עֻזִּ֥י (“rock of my strength”, oshb:Ps.62.8) echoes the prior row's own close. One verse in, register shifts to public exhortation: (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ ב֤וֹ בְכָל עֵ֨ת עָ֗ם “Trust in him at all times, you people” (web:Ps.62.8), closing on the psalm’s second Selah. The unit moves through the wisdom reflection on human vanity, “men of low degree are just a breath” (web:Ps.62.9), and the warning against riches (web:Ps.62.10), closing on the revelatory formula (oshb:Ps.62.12) אַחַ֤ת דִּבֶּ֬ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים שְׁתַּֽיִם “God has spoken once; twice I have heard this” (web:Ps.62.11).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating Ps.62.7-62.8 as a continuation of the preceding confidence refrain rather than a fresh public-facing unit was rejected, given the shift from first-person soul-address to plural imperative address.
observed_substrate_signals: Plural imperative address (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ opens the exhortation, marking the register shift from the preceding first-person ring.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.8 (oshb:Ps.62.9) — the psalm’s later of 2 Selah instances (sweep: 2 verses); no further Selah in web:Ps.62.9-web:Ps.62.12.
edited_rows.device_notes: The Hebrew word for "silence" opening (oshb:Ps.62.2) דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה recurs, from the same root, at the opening of oshb:Ps.65.2 (web:Ps.65.1) — shared vocabulary texture, not a boundary signal.

edited_rows.rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.63.0 = oshb:Ps.63.1) naming the desert-of-Judah setting. The strophe opens on a vocative, (oshb:Ps.63.2) אֱלֹהִ֤ים אֵלִ֥י אַתָּ֗ה “God, you are my God” (web:Ps.63.1), with a נפשי (“My soul”) occurrence already in the same verse, (oshb:Ps.63.2) צָמְאָ֬ה לְךָ֨ נַפְשִׁ֗י “My soul thirsts for you”. It moves through the sanctuary vision “So I have seen you in the sanctuary” (web:Ps.63.2) and closes on the resolve to bless, “I will lift up my hands in your name” (web:Ps.63.4).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through web:Ps.63.5 was rejected: the second כן inclusio-closer (oshb:Ps.63.5) falls inside this row's own span, at web:Ps.63.4, not beyond it; web:Ps.63.5 (oshb:Ps.63.6) opens instead with כמו (‘like/as’) and begins the psalm's sensory-satisfaction imagery that continues through Ps.63.8, not the sanctuary-vision material of Ps.63.2-63.4.
observed_substrate_signals: כן opens both oshb:Ps.63.3 and oshb:Ps.63.5 — an intra-row inclusio inside this row's own span (sweep: 2 verses in Ps 63); the next row's opening verse, oshb:Ps.63.6, opens instead with כמו (‘like/as’), a different word.
נפשי opens this row's own inclusio at (oshb:Ps.63.2) נַפְשִׁ֗י (sweep: 4 verses carry נפשי in Ps 63).
edited_rows.device_notes: The parent grouping for this row set is Psalm 63 whole.

edited_rows.rationale: The unit is bracketed by its own נפשי (“my soul”) pair: it opens (oshb:Ps.63.6) תִּשְׂבַּ֣ע נַפְשִׁ֑י “My soul shall be satisfied” (web:Ps.63.5) and closes (oshb:Ps.63.9) דָּבְקָ֣ה נַפְשִׁ֣י “My soul stays close to you” (web:Ps.63.8), moving through night-watch meditation (web:Ps.63.6) and the refuge image “the shadow of your wings” (web:Ps.63.7).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.63.7 instead of Ps.63.8 was rejected, since Ps.63.8's closing 'my soul' clause closes the same bracket that Ps.63.5's opening clause begins.
observed_substrate_signals: נפשי opens the span at (oshb:Ps.63.6) נַפְשִׁ֑י and closes it at (oshb:Ps.63.9) נַפְשִׁ֣י — an internal lexical inclusio, though not exclusive to this row's edges: the lexeme recurs once more just past this row's own close, at oshb:Ps.63.10 (web:Ps.63.9) — those who seek my soul.

edited_rows.rationale: An adversative pivot opens this unit away from the psalmist’s own voice: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה “But those who seek my soul to destroy it” (web:Ps.63.9), continuing through “They shall be jackal food” (web:Ps.63.10) to a second adversative, (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ “But the king shall rejoice in God” (web:Ps.63.11), the psalm’s closing verse.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the enemies' judgment (Ps.63.9-63.10) from the king's contrasting joy (Ps.63.11) into separate rows was rejected, since both share the adversative pivot away from the psalmist's own voice and no independent driver separates them.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה, glossed ‘but they’, opens the enemies’ judgment; (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ (“But the king”, web:Ps.63.11) opens the closing verse — two adversative openings inside a 3-verse unit.
נפשי recurs once more at (oshb:Ps.63.10) יְבַקְשׁ֣וּ נַפְשִׁ֑י, this psalm's 4th instance in Ps 63, now naming the object the enemies seek — an ironic reversal of the row at Ps.63.5-63.8.
